articles.title: Katie Taylor vs Flora Pili: Bray native determined to sign off on her career in style
articles.summary: Katie Taylor is preparing for a stern test from Flora Pili rather than a Croke Park testimonial on Saturday night as she seeks to sign off on her career in style.
articles.body:
Katie Taylor is preparing for a stern test from Flora Pili rather than a Croke Park testimonial on Saturday night as she seeks to sign off on her career in style.

Over 54 years will have passed since Muhammad Ali headlined the last boxing event at the home of the Gaelic Athletic Association.

Just as 'The Greatest' blazed a trail in a career that transcended sport, Taylor has done likewise.

Elevating women's boxing to heights never experienced or perhaps expected, the 40-year-old will make her final walk in front of 80,000 fans with the opportunity to become undisputed champion at light-welterweight once again.

It is all set up for the glorious farewell, and while talk about ring-walks and musical entertainment is a feature of fight week in Dublin, Taylor is looking no further than her 29-year-old French opponent, who is perfect through 12 fights and holds the European and IBO belt.

"I'm trying not to think about it as I have a job to do," Taylor, whose record stands at 25-1, said at Tuesday's news conference when the subject of the overall event was raised.

"It's too dangerous a sport to have your body in the ring and your heart out of it, thinking of retirement.

"I have a job to do, and I'm very much focused on that job. The most important part of Saturday night is I get my hand raised, so it's business as usual for me.

"I've a live opponent in front of me, so it won't be a walk in the park. She is here to win ... a young, undefeated fighter. It will be a tough fight, but that's when I'm at my best."

There is truth to that final statement as her best performances have come when the danger was at its greatest: in the victories over Amanda Serrano, the rematch against Chantelle Cameron and in a 2020 rematch against Delfine Persoon which came 14 months after a much tighter battle in New York.

Pili, perhaps not keen on brash statements, has arrived in Ireland with braided hair in the colours of the French flag, and while few outside of her camp are predicting the upset, there is a quiet confidence.

"We're all aware of the task ahead but have the whole of France behind us, so we will be proud to take on Katie," said Pili, who is aware there is everything to gain should she spoil the party.

"I've nothing to lose and everything to win. I'm the underdog, and there is no pressure on me, so I will give everything I can from the first bell and take home all of these belts."

'Taylor has to focus on the fight' - Hearn

Taylor's sole career defeat came at the hands of Cameron in Dublin back in 2023 - a loss she later avenged to become undisputed champion in a second division - so there is certainly a realisation this is not a foregone conclusion on Saturday.

Undoubtedly, Cameron - whose only defeat came in that rematch against Taylor - has proven herself as a bona fide elite fighter, a status Pili is yet to reach.

While promoter Eddie Hearn is predicting "one of the greatest moments Irish sport has ever seen" on Saturday night, that will only fully come to pass should Taylor prevail.

"She's got to focus on the fight, because this girl's decent," said the Matchroom boss.

"I'm not saying she's got the pedigree of Katie Taylor, but Katie's 40 years old. She's [Taylor] fighting a young, strong girl who likes to trade, and so does Katie, who's IBO world champion, European champion, a decent amateur who can become undisputed herself on Saturday.

"She [Taylor] was saying, 'I need to prepare myself for war here', because she can't walk out, then get in the ring, and then it just passes you by, because that can happen.

"It will be an all-out war, because it's the only way she knows how to fight. She's not going to try to box and move because she'll want to leave it all in the ring."

Taylor is certainly making all the right noises in that regard and has been as methodical as ever in camp.

While she accepts it is "hard to prepare yourself for a moment I haven't experienced before" in terms of the overall occasion, she is determined to add one final glorious chapter to an already remarkable legacy.

"I'm not sure how I'm going to feel, but it will be a special night," she added.

"I'm going to walk to the ring, focus on the fight, as there will be plenty of time after to reflect on this amazing career, should I get my hand raised.

"I wouldn't be human if I didn't think of it all and think of all the little girls who may be at a boxing event for the first time.

"In my mind's eye, I think of one of those girls who might fall in love with this beautiful sport and may even surpass my achievements, all because of one amazing September day in Croke Park. I can't wait to hear those stories."

articles.title: Moses Itauma preparations questioned after defeat to Filip Hrgovic but heavyweight star is backed to become world champion
articles.summary: 'He didn't spar enough!' - Delicious Orie and Sam Noakes have queried if Moses Itauma did all he could in the build-up to his IBF world heavyweight title loss at the hands of unfancied Filip Hrgovic
articles.body:
Itauma was the overwhelming favourite heading into the bout but having dominated the opening eight rounds dramatically ran out of gas as he was stopped in the ninth.

Delicious Orie admits he was surprised by Itauma's pre-fight admission that he had not before sparred 12 rounds.

"It was experience. If I was getting a ring and knowing I've got 12 rounds ahead of me, I'm doing 15 rounds. For me, not doing 12 rounds going into a 12-round fight is crazy," he told Sky Sports.

"I guess it's each to their own. Moses boxed so perfectly but it was gradual rather than sudden. It goes back to experience. Hrgovic won that night because of it.

"He blew a gasket. This reminded me of new boxers in a new era taking strength and conditioning so seriously. You've got to find out about yourself before you get into the ring. You cannot learn on the job when it comes to professional boxing.

"I think he should have beaten Hrgovic. I wasn't in his training camps, but we've all heard it. He didn't spar enough; it's as simple as that. Just because you can lift weights or run fast does not mean you can sustain a 12-round fight. It's a completely different beast."

Like Itauma, lightweight contender Sam Noakes hails from Kent and has world title ambitions.

He agreed with Orie that inexperience contributed to Itauma's first career defeat, with the 21-year-old having to be taken to hospital following the fight.

"I think it was more Itauma beating himself. With all the success he was having, I think he might have just gone a little too fast out of the blocks. He wasn't out of his depth at all. It was more that he got tired and obviously Hrgovic capitalised on it," said Noakes.

"If he'd done a 12-rounder before maybe it might have helped. It's all well and good in hindsight but he was blasting out serious level opponents. That was the next step for him. He just came up short in a world title fight at 21. That's boxing unfortunately."

Itauma was bidding to become the second youngest man behind Mike Tyson to become world heavyweight champion.

However, having stopped all his opponents inside six rounds before facing Hrgovic, some have questioned whether the rising prospect was rushed into world title contention.

Orie disagrees with that notion and believes his promoter Frank Warren is the perfect man to help rebuild his career.

"I don't think he was being rushed. I think that was a good step up with Hrgovic. I do think there was a lot of hype. I don't think it would have had a massive impact on the fight. Itauma doesn't strike me as someone who loves all that hype. He's just a normal guy from Kent," he stated.

"Frank will more than anybody else know what the best thing is to do. I think his mindset is the question here. In his mind, his world's fallen apart. What he does in the next one or two years will be the deciding factor in my opinion for the rest of his boxing career."

Despite the setback, both Orie and Noakes are confident Itauma will recover and become world heavyweight champion in the future.

"One thing Itauma does have is the greatest asset known to man: time. 21 years old, he has a lot of time in front of him and depending on his mindset, this is just the beginning. This is part of becoming a world champion," Orie said.

"We've seen it time and time again with the likes of David Haye and [Wladimir] Klitschko losing in their early to mid-20s. It's the standard process.

"People just think it's smooth sailing, you turn professional, you beat Mike Tyson's record, you become world champion and retire into the sunset. Boxing doesn't work like that unfortunately and we've seen it here."

Meanwhile, Noakes added: "The experience everyone was saying he lacked, he has now gained. When he comes back, he'll be even better. As a fighter, the loss is terrible. It's like the end of the world.

"My advice to him would be just get back in the mix as quick as you can and back onto that world title chase. I have no doubt the ending will still be the same; he'll still be undisputed heavyweight champion."

articles.title: Kofi, Austin Creed reveal they were blindsided by WWE, asked to take 'more than 50%' pay cut
articles.summary: WWE legends Kofi Kingston and Xavier Woods — now Kofi and Austin Creed in AEW — clear the air on their messy WWE departure and how much of a pay cut they wer...
articles.body:
AEW All In 2026 delivered as one of the year's best professional wrestling events this past Sunday in London. On the grand stage of the world-famous Wembley Stadium, one of the annual spectacle's biggest moments was the debut of Kofi and Austin Creed — now known as The New Level after spending years in WWE as Kofi Kingston and Xavier Woods of The New Day.

The legendary duo wasn't advertised for the pay-per-view event, but instead made their arrival as a surprise entrant in the promotion's first-ever Trios Roulette Royale match for the AEW Trios Championships. Alongside Swerve Strickland, Kofi and Creed pulled off the win to become the new champions on only their first night on the job.

Kofi and Creed parted ways with WWE in a shocking development in May after a 12-year run teaming together, in addition to teaming with Big E. While Big E remained with the company as a retired wrestler-turned-analyst, Kofi and Creed were asked to take significant pay cuts when it came time to negotiate their contracts.

Speaking on Monday's edition of "The Ariel Helwani Show," they revealed that they only officially signed with AEW a day before All In. Regarding their WWE departure, the reported 50% pay-cut ask was incorrect: it was higher, according to Kofi.

"We just thought the terms that they wanted us to perform under were not fair based on what we brought to the table, based on what we're worth, based on the knowledge and prowess we have as performers and wrestlers," Kofi told Uncrowned. "What we can give back to the younger people and do in entertainment. Being able to go out there and garner a reaction as good guys or bad guys, no matter the situation. We took a lot of great pride in being Swiss Army knives. Whatever the situation was, we would make it great and make it entertaining. Compensation was definitely a big part, for sure, but more so, we wanted to work.

"I will say, it was more than 50%. It was more. The compensation is a big part of it, for sure, but the bigger part is being able to go out and live your dream in a way you want to live it out and be appreciated for it. We took it all into consideration, and we knew this was the only path to take."

Creed chimed in afterward when asked if there were any farewell messages from his longtime wrestling home. "Nope," he said when asked whether he received any thank-yous or calls upon leaving the company.

The process of adjusting to post-WWE life hit The New Level immediately, and even now, Kofi still struggles to call his longtime best friend "Creed" rather than "Woods" after having to leave the "Xavier Woods" name behind in WWE.

There was plenty of uncertainty in the early stages of their unemployment, said Kofi, who hadn't been a free agent in 20 years.

"This is so arrogant to say, but I'm just going to say it. I don't mean it in, like, a cocky way, but when you have the caliber of the career that we've had collectively as a group, you feel like you would not have to be in a position where you'd have to like, go in bet on yourselves again. But here we were," Kofi said.

"We found ourselves in that exact position, and as a father, if we didn't try to do this, if we didn't follow our hearts, how can I go back and tell my kids to go follow their dreams? To believe in themselves. To block out what people are saying about you and how they feel about you, and believe in yourself.

"If we didn't do that, I would feel like such a hypocrite, and I know Woods — Creed — feels the same way. That's going to take awhile; this time I caught myself. I had to change his name in my phone and everything. Like, bro, it's been a process. It's really trying to recalculate and recalibrate, but that's also a beautiful part of the whole process is being able to be reborn in a way. From a career standpoint, from a standpoint of having fun, from the standpoint of the uncertainty."

Ultimately, AEW was always the perfect landing spot for the all-time great tag team, said Creed. They never spoke to any other company before signing, largely because of the great tag scene AEW has cultivated throughout its existence.

In WWE, the tag-team division typically goes through waves of value for the company, and at its highest point in the past 15 years, Kofi and Creed were at the forefront. Injuries to their trio and the divisional fluctuation changed that, as they — and every other team — fell down the totem pole in recent years.

At AEW All In, specifically, the tag division was put on full display with a single image, coming directly after the current champions and all-time greats, Christian Cage and Adam Copeland, successfully defended against The Young Bucks.

"When it came to tag-team wrestling, it really wasn't a priority [in WWE], so we looked across the pond and saw the Bucks, FTR, Cope and Christian, Private Party, The Dogs, all these tag-teams having bangers," Kofi said. "'Man, what if we could be involved with that?' They look like they're having so much fun. You watch AEW pay-per-views, and I'm jumping out of my seat like a fan again. It excites me to watch that show.

"We're thinking, 'What if we could be part of that and add ourselves as one of, if not the greatest tag-team in history?' That was really the determining factor. Let's go and try to do what we love to do and feel passionate about our craft and feel like we're able to give in a way that is significant and matters. To go have bangers every night. That's what this is supposed to be. You're not supposed to go to work and feel frustrated with whatever is going on. You want to be able to have time to have matches that are incredible and entertaining. That's what the goal was."

Creed added to Kofi's sentiment as he examined the landscape in AEW. Despite holding WWE tag-team gold 12 times, there is still plenty more he sees for their future.

With all the fresh options at their disposal, it really is a tag-team playground of riches.

"We have a lot of friends over there, a lot of good people who said a lot of good things about it. But again, I know we probably sound like broken records to go back to the idea of having such a robust tag division and that being what our real focus is in this," Creed said.

"It just made a lot of sense to us, because watching those matches, watching those stories they get to tell — nobody is really doing it like that for tag-team wrestling. So it really just makes a lot of sense for us in that respect.

"I genuinely believe that this is the best tag-team division possibly ever. Like that shot at All In of all the tag-teams in the ring, that's some of the greatest tag-teams, I think, of our generation, so, possibly, when we're all done, maybe of all time, you know? And when are we going to get a chance to do something like that again? When has anyone ever done that in actuality? So, it really feels like, for the next duration, tag-team wrestling is going to be — they're eating well if they love tag wrestling."

articles.title: "¿Creen que Topuria va a correr el riesgo de pelear contra Usman Nurmagomedov?"
articles.standfirst: Dan Hooker cree que 'El Matador' declinaría una pelea contra el primo de Khabib para darle la bienvenida a la compañía
articles.summary: Dan Hooker cree que 'El Matador' declinaría una pelea contra el primo de Khabib para darle la bienvenida a la compañía
articles.body: Este fin de semana, Dan Hooker (24-14) será el enemigo público número uno de Francia en el UFC París, donde se medirá a Salahdine Parnasse (23-2) en el debut del galo de la compañía. Parnasse llega con el cartel de superestrella directamente en un combate estelar contra un tipo muy experimentado, que ha desvelado que nadie más quería asumir el riesgo dentro del top 15 de peso ligero. De hecho, augura que sucederá lo mismo con Usman Nurmagomedov, dejando un recado para Ilia Topuria y para el resto de peleadores de la categoría. Muchos conocerán a Parnasse porque recientemente peleó en la cartelera de MVP, compañía de Jake Paul, donde finalizó a Kenny Cross en el primer asalto. Sin embargo, el peleador francés tiene mucho más bagaje en su carrera, ya que ha sido doble campeón en KSW en peso pluma y peso ligero, e incluso llegó a pelear por el título de peso wélter pero perdió por decisión. Un coco al que nadie quería enfrentar, salvo el neozelandés. Según él, algo similar ocurrirá si Usman Nurmagomedov acaba fichando por la UFC. El primo de Khabib Nurmagomedov es el actual campeón de peso ligero de PFL, y ahora que ha finalizado su contrato se rumorea que podría fichar por la promotora dirigida por Dana White. Sin embargo, Hooker cree que ninguno de los peleadores top estará dispuesto a darle la bienvenida. "La gente dice 'oh, Usman va a entrar y va a pelear contra Topuria'. Que se jodan. Que sean serios. ¿Creen que Ilia va a correr el riesgo de pelear contra un tipo no rankeado que ni siquiera es de la UFC? Nadie más quiere correr el riesgo. Esa es la misma razón por la que yo fui el tipo que peleó contra Chandler. Es la misma razón por la que me pagan dinero para pelear contra Parnasse, porque ninguno de estos otros tipos de la división quiere arriesgarse por el premio. Llaman a Dan Hooker, le ofrecen un poco de dinero por el peligro y él da la bienvenida a estos chicos a las grandes ligas", afirmó en una entrevista con 'Submission Radio' Hooker es lo que se conoce como un hombre de compañía. Un peleador que sabe que es prácticamente imposible que sea campeón, y que si le ponen sobre la mesa el dinero suficiente no duda en subirse al octágono contra quien sea. Ya lo hizo contra Michael Chandler en su momento y acabó siendo noqueado, pero con 'Hangman' la acción está asegurada. El neozelandés se ha enfrentado a otros grandes nombres como Dustin Poirier o Islam Makhachev, y en la mayoría de sus combates el bono de la noche está asegurado. Además, en otra entrevista con RMC ha revelado que este cheque será el más grande de su carrera. "Si me pagan tanto dinero por pelear contra los nuevos chicos, entonces pelearé contra los nuevos chicos hasta el día en que me muera. Pelearía contra Francis Ngannou por la cantidad de dinero que me están pagando. Es el pago más grande de mi carrera, sin duda", finalizó. Actualmente, Hooker ocupa el puesto número 10 en el ránking de peso ligero, mientras que Parnasse es debutante, por lo que tiene mucho que perder a nivel competitivo. Eso sí, la UFC suele premiar este tipo de actitudes, por lo que en caso de ganar seguramente tenga la opción de medirse a un peleador de la parte alta del ránking para volver a entrar en la conversación titular.

articles.title: Katie Taylor vs Flora Pili: Irish boxing legend reflects on historic Croke Park farewell - and pokes fun at Tyson Fury
articles.summary: Katie Taylor says she is "not like Tyson Fury" and will only retire once ahead of her final fight; the Irish boxer faces mandatory challenger Flora Pili in a swansong bout at a sold-out Croke Park in Dublin
articles.body:
Taylor (25-1-0, 6 KOs) is set to fight mandatory contender Flora Pili in front of a sell-out 82,000 crowd at Croke Park in Dublin in her last ever professional fight, and she has the chance to end her career as the undisputed lightweight champion.

Unlike some other professional boxers, Taylor has assured her fans she only intends to retire once:

"I think it's important to have a bit left when you bow out," Taylor told Sky Sports.

"You always have that itch, but I don't think I'm going to be the type of fighter who goes in and out of retirement like Tyson Fury does.

"How many times has he actually been retired - maybe five or six times?

"When it's my time to go out, I'm just going to enjoy the fruits of my labour."

A trailblazer for women's boxing, Taylor's career has spanned 25 years since her first amateur bout in 2001, featuring an Olympic gold medal, a headline fight at Madison Square Garden, and two separate reigns as an undisputed champion along the way.

The prospect of bowing out with a third undisputed title by beating an undefeated challenger at her home country's most iconic sporting venue is a prospect that even Taylor herself considers too good to be true.

"Croke Park is part of Irish culture, and I'm so proud of Croke Park myself.

"I said after my last fight: 'what could be bigger than headlining at Madison Square Garden?'

"The only thing that could be bigger now is headlining Croke Park, and I have the privilege now of actually doing that.

"It's been very, very difficult over the last few years, politically, to actually get this fight over the line, and here we are, and we're only maybe six weeks away from this fight, and I have a chance to end this amazing journey in our best arena.

"I'm actually nearly pinching myself sometimes when I actually talk about it."

Oleksandr Uysk - a figure of similar unassailable stature in men's boxing - chose to vacate his belts to choose his own 'final chapter' and avoid a fight against mandatory challenger Agit Kabayel earlier this year.

Taylor, in contrast, opted for the hard way out, with a fight against Pili (12-0-0, 2 KOs) perhaps the most challenging she could have accepted.

But that attitude to take on all comers is typical of Taylor, and exactly what has got her to this point in her career and endeared her to much of the boxing public.

"I didn't want one of those easy fights," Taylor said. "I wanted someone who was going to challenge me.

"I wanted a hungry young fighter and that's exactly who we have with Flora Pili. I know I have to be at my very, very best for this fight and I plan on putting on a career-best performance as well. That's what I'm training for.

"I love the fact I have a real threat in front of me. I don't think anybody could ever say, throughout my whole career, that I've ever ducked anybody - I think I've always fought the toughest fights."

Taylor's historic outing Croke Park underlines her status on hallowed ground as a boxer - it will be the first fight at the Gaelic games arena since Muhammad Ali's fought Al 'Blue' Lewis, 54 years ago in 1972.

"Ending my career in Croke Park is really is beyond anything I could have actually dreamt of.

"I dreamt of becoming an Olympic champion as a kid, and that dream came to pass. But these last 10 years [as a professional, I didn't even have the capacity to dream these things.

"I'm just so grateful that I've had this amazing career. The Irish people have supported me from the get-go, and I'm so grateful for that.

"I'm so proud that I'm Irish, I'm so proud I get to represent this amazing country, and I get a chance now to fight one more time in front of my home crowd."

articles.title: Katie Taylor: Five sliding doors moments that shaped her legendary career
articles.summary: From writing a letter to her idol as a 10-year-old to messaging a promoter on social media, here are five sliding doors moments that helped shape Katie Taylor’s career.
articles.body:
On Saturday, Katie Taylor steps through the ropes at an 82,000-capacity Croke Park to face France's Flora Pili in her farewell fight.

Victory on the hallowed Dublin turf would write one final fairytale chapter - a chance to bow out as undisputed light-welterweight champion and put the seal on a career that has revolutionised women's sport.

There have been countless moments that have shaped the 40-year-old's journey.

From a childhood letter to a Twitter direct message, these are five sliding doors moments in the making of an Irish icon.

Long before Taylor became Olympic champion, she was a 10-year-old girl in Bray who simply wanted to box.

There was nowhere for her to go though. Women's boxing was unsanctioned in Ireland, absent from the Olympic programme and devoid of any clear professional pathway.

But there was Deirdre Gogarty. Having relocated to the United States, she became Ireland's first female professional world champion in 1997 when she defeated Bonnie Canino for the WIBF featherweight title in Louisiana.

"How did you do it when everyone tried to stop you?" a 10-year-old Taylor asked in a letter sent to her hero.

"If you keep working at it and keep showing your skills, somebody's going to say 'we've got to let this girl box'," Gogarty replied.

Reflecting on the letter years later, Gogarty added: "It's mind-blowing. Especially when she wrote, 'maybe one day they'll let us box in the Olympics'."

Had that letter never been written, Taylor might still have found her way to the top, but Gogarty offered hope when none seemingly existed.

Heartbreak at Rio 2016 and the leap into the unknown

When the International Olympic Committee was undecided on including women's boxing at the Games, Taylor was brought in for showcase events in front of sceptical officials in Chicago. Her dazzling displays dismantled every argument.

"Katie won't say this, and I've been holding back from saying this, but single-handedly, Katie Taylor got women's boxing into the Olympics," her manager Brian Peters says.

Women's boxing made its Olympic debut at the London 2012 Games and Taylor claimed lightweight gold.

Four years later in Rio, however, that amateur journey ended when a split-decision quarter-final defeat shattered Taylor's title defence. She was at a crossroads - rebuild for another Olympic cycle or turn professional in an era where women's pro boxing was still neglected.

"It was probably the worst year of my career," Taylor later admitted. "I needed a change. I needed a new mindset."

Had she secured a second Olympic gold, the motivation to dive into the pro ranks might have evaporated. Instead, the sting of defeat forced reinvention.

Turning professional was one thing, but securing both the right team and commercial backing was another challenge.

First came manager Peters, who initially stepped in out of concern for her future.

"I only took her on not to see her end up with people who didn't know what they were doing," Peters says.

On 4 October 2016, Taylor sent Matchroom's Eddie Hearn a direct message on Twitter, now known as X, asking if he would consider promoting her. Hearn replied 24 hours later, inviting Taylor, Peters, and her mother Bridget to a London restaurant. Hearn even borrowed his father's car to impress Taylor.

The charm offensive worked and Taylor made her debut at Wembley Arena a month later.

In a sport notorious for fractured relationships and bitter splits, Taylor's core team has remained the same from day one with Peters, Hearn and trainer Ross Enamait.

"In a business full of egos, she's stayed loyal to everyone around her and remained the most humble person you could ever meet," Peters says.

Had Hearn dismissed that DM - or had Taylor lacked the enduring loyalty that kept the same tight-knit team in her corner for a decade - the promotional engine that transformed women's boxing might never have started.

By April 2022, Taylor was the undisputed lightweight champion. She had already survived a razor-thin majority decision against Delfine Persoon at Madison Square Garden (MSG) three years earlier to unify - a night when many felt her aura of invincibility was almost cracked.

Returning to MSG to face seven-division title winner Amanda Serrano presented a different magnitude of threat.

Their blockbuster marked the first time two women headlined the storied New York venue. In front of a sellout crowd of 19,187, Taylor claimed a split-decision victory in what was widely hailed as the fight of the year.

Had one scorecard leaned the other way or had the bout failed to deliver on its enormous hype, the momentum behind women's mega-fights would have stalled.

Instead, the victory spawned a record-breaking rivalry. Their 2024 rematch drew global viewing figures on Netflix on the undercard of Jake Paul v Mike Tyson, before Taylor sealed the trilogy at the Garden in 2025.

Taylor's first professional defeat came in May 2023 at Dublin's 3Arena when she was outpointed by Chantelle Cameron for the undisputed light-welterweight belts.

At 36, questions around retirement surfaced.

In the ring immediately following the defeat, Peters says he told his fighter to congratulate Cameron and ask for the rematch.

Six months later, Taylor delivered a masterclass in grit, claiming a majority decision to become a two-weight undisputed champion.

"The pressure was immense," Peters says.

"For all she had done, her legacy was suddenly questioned. Had Chantelle won the rematch, who knows what would have happened?"

Croke Park is not really a sixth sliding door but rather the final pay-off.

After beating Serrano in last year's trilogy decider, Taylor quietly decided she was done.

"She actually retired that night," Peters says. "She said, 'We convincingly beat Serrano - where do we go from there?' I said I'll agree on one condition."

That condition was Croke Park or nothing.

"Croke Park - no disrespect to Wembley - is the greatest stadium in the world," Peters says. "You cut an Irish person and they'll bleed Croke Park."

Peters insists there will be no change of heart - no Cameron trilogy and no comebacks.

"When Katie gives her word, that is it," he says.

Regardless of Saturday's result, Taylor will be remembered as a pioneer who kicked open the door for women's boxing.

articles.title: UFC: Alex Pereira's Aline Pereira sister to fight for UFC contract in October
articles.summary: Aline Pereira, who has a mixed MMA record, will fight for the chance to win a UFC contract on Dana White's Contender Series in October.
articles.body:
Aline Pereira is set to fight for a UFC contract that would see her join her brother and two-weight UFC champion Alex Pereira in the MMA promotion.

Aline will fight undefeated prospect Smilla Sundell, a Muay Thai champion in the Asia-based ONE Championship, on Dana White's Contender Series in Las Vegas on 13 October.

UFC president White's Contender Series offers a chance for fighters outside the UFC to win contracts in one-off contests.

Pereira, who currently holds a 3-2 record, with all three of her victories coming by decision, confirmed on her Instagram she will face Sweden's Sundell in a bantamweight bout.

The 35-year-old's most recent victory was a split decision against Jade Masson-Wong in May, on the undercard of Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions's first MMA event.

He was dragged 60ft under a bus - now he's fighting for a UFC contract

Mir suffers shock defeat as Clancy Jr wins UFC contract

Several siblings have fought in the UFC together, including Nick and Nate Diaz, but a sister-brother duo is more rare.

Melissa Martinez and David Martinez made history in 2024 when they became the first sister and brother to compete in the UFC at the same time.

Just like her brother, Pereira enjoyed a successful kickboxing career.

Her fights included a super-bantamweight title opportunity with Glory promotions, before she transitioned to MMA in 2022.

Pereira decided to step away from the sport in 2023 after her MMA career began with a rocky 1‑2 spell with Legacy Fighting Alliance (LFA).

She found momentum in Karate Combat League, going 3‑0 with two knockouts and winning the promotion's inaugural women's flyweight title in 2024.

The Brazilian returned to MMA in late 2025 and is often seen being trained and cornered by her brother, Alex.

Alex failed in his bid to become a three-weight UFC champion in June, losing to Frenchman Ciryl Gane in an interim heavyweight title fight.

Aline faces a tough opponent in Sundell, who has two wins in her MMA career to date.

The 21‑year‑old signed with ONE Championship in 2022 and won its inaugural women's strawweight Muay Thai title at just 17 years and 161 days old, becoming the promotion's youngest ever champion.

articles.title: Usman Nurmagomedov's latest Instagram story with Dana White goes viral hours after UFC President says he “crossed the line” at UFC Shanghai
articles.summary: MMA News: Usman Nurmagomedov has seemingly responded to the controversy surrounding his actions at UFC Shanghai. Just hours after UFC CEO Dana White said the PF.
articles.body: Usman Nurmagomedov has seemingly responded to the controversy surrounding his actions at UFC Shanghai. Just hours after UFC CEO Dana White said the PFL lightweight champion had “crossed a line” by jumping the cage, Usman shared an Instagram story featuring himself with White. The Dagestani fighter added the caption “real men”, creating a striking contrast with the criticism he had received following his older brother Umar Nurmagomedov’s knockout loss to Song Yadong.The post comes after a tense night in Shanghai. Usman jumped over the cage immediately after seeing Umar knocked out in the second round. His emotional reaction violated a long-standing MMA rule that prevents cornermen from entering the cage before officials allow them inside. White later made it clear that he did not approve of Usman’s actions.Usman Nurmagomedov shares pictures with Dana White after UFC Shanghai controversyThe controversy began after Song Yadong stopped Umar Nurmagomedov in the second round of their UFC Shanghai main event.Umar suffered the first knockout loss of his professional career. The result visibly affected his younger brother Usman Nurmagomedov, who was watching from outside the cage.In an emotional moment, Usman jumped over the cage and moved toward his unconscious brother. However, cornermen are not allowed to enter the cage until a commission or event official opens the door.The incident quickly attracted attention from the MMA community.Dana White was eventually asked about Usman’s actions during the Contender Series press conference. The UFC boss did not hide his disagreement.“Yeah, what do you mean by how he reacted? He definitely did (cross a line)… I would agree with that”, White said.White’s comments came only hours before Usman posted his Instagram story with the UFC CEO.The image showed Usman alongside White, with the PFL champion adding the words “real men” as the caption.The post could be viewed as a sign that there is no serious personal tension between the two men. It may also suggest that Usman understands White’s position despite the criticism.Usman’s actions in Shanghai were not the first time he has jumped into the cage without waiting for permission.He previously did the same after Islam Makhachev defeated Dustin Poirier at UFC 302 in Newark. Usman entered the cage to celebrate with Makhachev before being escorted away by security.Former UFC middleweight champion Chris Weidman believes the repeated incidents should have consequences.“He should be in trouble, 100 percent, from the commission for jumping the cage and acting like that. If we have cornermen jumping into the octagon, it’s not good… He shouldn’t have been there”, Weidman said on Paramount+’s Deep Waters podcast.However, Song Yadong offered a more understanding view.“But watching the slow motion, it looked like he was turning around to throw an elbow or something,” Song Yadong stated. “But actually, I understand because they are brothers, you know.”For now, it remains unclear whether Usman will face any punishment for the Shanghai incident.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Dubois vs Wardley 2: Fabio Wardley says there will be "zero excuses" for his rematch with Daniel Dubois
articles.summary: Fabio Wardley says there are "zero excuses" heading into his highly anticipated rematch with WBO heavyweight champion Daniel Dubois on 17 October.
articles.body:
Fabio Wardley says there are "zero excuses" heading into his highly anticipated rematch with WBO heavyweight champion Daniel Dubois on 17 October as he looks to write a new chapter in his story.

Wardley, 31, dropped fellow Briton Dubois twice when they fought in May but was stopped in round 11 and lost his world title.

The Ipswich fighter immediately triggered his rematch clause and will look to avenge the only defeat of his career at London's O2 Arena.

"I have zero excuses for the loss on the night and zero excuses going into the rematch," Wardley said at Wednesday's launch news conference.

"It's just another chapter in the story that is my career.

"By no means did I expect to get through boxing unscathed - not many do. Even Daniel has proven you can take a loss and come back, he's a two-time heavyweight champion."

Dubois was coming off the third defeat of his 26-fight career when he showed courage to twice get off the canvas to overcome Wardley.

The 28-year-old, who also held the IBF title in 2024, vowed to seize his opportunity to build momentum with another victory as he looks to unify in 2027.

"I was coming off a defeat so I was a bit nervous. It's a fresh start for me," said Dubois.

"I want to be the last man standing and be up there with the greats."

October's rematch was announced on Saturday at the O2 Arena when Dubois and Wardley faced off in the ring moments before Moses Itauma's defeat by Filip Hrgovic for the IBF heavyweight title.

Dubois and Wardley both said on Wednesday that they had a new-found respect for each other after going through a gruelling 11 rounds earlier in the year.

But there was a tense moment when they faced off at the news conference, with Wardley asking "can we be cool?" before Dubois responded "after the fight, man".

A confused-looking Wardley said: "Do you not like me? I thought after the fight we were all right?"

There were several awkward moments in the build-up to their first bout, with Dubois refusing Wardley's fist bump, and there was a similar situation when they crossed paths backstage before their latest media engagement.

Reflecting on their first meeting, Wardley said he has learned from his mistakes and will ensure they are corrected.

"I lost a bit of, not to say the old me, but I felt a bit too comfortable with the really early knockdown followed by another in the third. I relaxed into the fight thinking I've done it twice and I can get him out of there," Wardley said.

"I think I was a victim of my own success and got trigger happy. I was carried away with launching my right hand and trying to finish it.

"I was too relaxed, comfortable and laid back in certain scenarios."

Dubois kept his answers short, insisting he is not looking beyond Wardley, but Queensberry chief Frank Warren painted a picture of how bright the future might look for the winner.

Queensberry have built a strong stable of heavyweights over recent years and have three of the four world champions in their ranks.

Alongside WBO champion Dubois, Warren has WBC champion Agit Kabayel and newly crowned IBF title-holder Filip Hrgovic.

Warren's intention is to keep those belts in-house and he plans to ensure they are all active in 2027.

"We'll be working hard to make the unifications - that's our plan," Warren said.

"Next year it's about getting them all together. We're doing something that even Don King didn't do. They are fighting regularly in big fights."

articles.title: Chantelle Cameron says talks are 'advanced' to fight Claressa Shields following victory over Mikaela Mayer
articles.summary: Chantelle Cameron beat Mikaela Mayer 97-93, 97-93, 96-94 on the judges' scorecards; She says a fight with Claressa Shields is now on the cards with talks advancing; Shields last said her preferred opponent would be Lauren Price
articles.body:
Cameron defeated Mayer by unanimous decision in a thriller to become WBA, WBC and WBO super-welterweight world champion at MPW-06 in Birmingham on Saturday.

She emerged victorious, edging a tight contest 97-93, 97-93, 96-94 on the judges' scorecards, further glossing a stellar resume that already honours her as the only woman to ever defeat the great Katie Taylor in her professional career.

With the victory strengthening Cameron's claim to a place among the greats of the women's game, she now has eyes on taking on the self-proclaimed 'GWOAT' [Greatest woman of all time] in Shields.

Many thought a rematch with Mayer would be next on her list, but Cameron told Sky Sports that things are moving rapidly with the WBC and WBA middleweight champion, who has a record of 19-0 across multiple weight divisions.

"I fancy [fighting] Clarissa Shields. I think I really do want to dare to be great and Clarissa Shields, she's the GWOAT, she's No 1 and that's going to be a fight that will just be unbelievable.

"The teams are actually in talks for that now so there is actually movement on that fight and for me that makes me giddy because I think that really is me challenging the very, very best and what an opportunity if this fight comes off.

"They [talks] are very advanced; it is moving pretty quick is what my managers told me, and it is a very high possibility the fight will happen."

Dmitriy Salita, Shields' promoter, confirmed that Cameron was firmly in contention for the fight.

Speaking exclusively to Sky Sports , Salita said: "Yes, Chantelle is under serious consideration as Claressa's next opponent. Claressa wants to fight the best, and Chantelle is unquestionably one of the elite pound-for-pound fighters in women's boxing. We are exploring the opportunity now, but it is too early to confirm a date.

"Absolutely [we are open to talks with MVP]. Our responsibility to the fighters we represent - and to the fans - is to do everything possible to make the best fights and create the biggest events. That is what being fighter-first means.

"Our track record demonstrates that we have worked with virtually every major promoter to make important fights, so working with MVP is certainly not an issue from our side. We also promote several of the best female fighters in the world, in addition to Claressa, and many of those fighters are involved in co-promotions with Claressa Shields' promotion.

"Definitely [Shields would welcome the challenge]. She has made that very clear on social media, and we have also had several conversations about it. Claressa wants to fight the best, and Chantelle represents exactly that kind of challenge."

Back when Shields beat Kaye Scott in the sixth round to reclaim those belts in August, it was discussed that her next preferred opponent would be Lauren Price.

Indeed, Shields said she would like this fight to take place between December and January.

It is a fight that Price has also welcomed, but Salita, believes the "mega" event "belongs in the United States.

articles.title: Oleksandr Gvozdyk reveals 'different' reality of Zuffa Boxing after abrupt release
articles.summary: Ex-champ Gvozdyk is one of the first victims of Zuffa's lose-and-you're-fired clause, mirroring the roster-cut philosophy UFC has long been associated with.
articles.body:
On Feb. 1, Oleksandr Gvozdyk dropped Radivoje Kalajdzic twice in the first six rounds of their light heavyweight contest inside Las Vegas' Meta Apex.

The 39-year-old Ukrainian — six fights into his career comeback — built the kind of lead that should have set up a routine points win against the challenger. But by the end of the seventh, he'd been dropped twice himself and stopped on his feet.

This was Gvozdyk's Zuffa Boxing debut, and it ended not in celebration, but in the first cracks of what would become a quiet, corporate unravelling.

Two months later, an email arrived in his inbox. No phone call, no meeting — just notice that the newest promotional company on the circuit no longer required his services. It proved to be the first example of Zuffa Boxing's much-maligned lose-and-you're-fired clause, mirroring the roster-cut philosophy the UFC has long been associated with. In April, Zuffa Boxing also ended its agreement with Robert Meriwether after his loss to Tony Hirsch Jr.

"They just executed their rights according to the contract," Gvozdyk told Uncrowned. "They don't owe me anything and never promised me anything.

"I lost the fight, and I'm almost 40 years old — other promoters didn't even sign me. Zuffa did. And I understand the reality: it's a growing company, signing fighters with a name to attract more attention. But no one promised to babysit me. They're just moving on."

It would be easy — tempting, even — to write this up as a straightforward tale of ruthless corporate boxing eating one of its own. Gvozdyk, to his credit, refuses to let you. But that doesn't mean the former WBC light heavyweight champion, a man who once stopped Adonis Stevenson to win a world title, isn't without grievances.

This cutthroat approach to promoter-fighter relationships isn't particularly new in the sport, it's just louder, clearer, literally written in black and white within a Zuffa contract. Almost in the image of Dana White, it's brash and unapologetic.

"Zuffa has a different approach compared to other promotional companies," he explained. "Where usually there's one person taking care of 10 tasks; at Zuffa they have 10 people for one task, and it seems like they don't communicate with each other — or maybe they just make it look that way. It's more of a corporate style. The rules are stricter. And if you want to change something, you have to get approval from a bunch of people who don't seem to have the authority to make their own decisions — they always have to ask someone else."

At age 39, coming off his second loss in three fights, Gvozdyk isn't naive about why he was let go. But the shape that it took after his February defeat clearly annoyed him, leaving him with unanswered questions.

"Regarding me, I was never promised anything beyond my contract. They sent me an offer through my manager, and I took it," he said.

"Again, it's a little different from what we're all used to. Basically, in real life it's the same as with other promoters — just more straightforward, with less hypocrisy. I'm talking about my case specifically — I assume the level of your stardom determines the strictness of the rules.

"After my loss, the Zuffa people I communicated with told me they liked my performance despite the outcome, and that we'd be looking at a comeback for late May or June. And I actually believed them — I think they probably believed it too. But, as I said, it seems to me Zuffa has a different business structure, with a clear hierarchy."

This confusion was evident throughout the months following his loss to Kalajdzic, in particular in regards to a post-fight drug test.

"There was an interesting moment — a week before I received the release letter, a random doping test came to me," he continued. "That's weird, because I've been in this business long enough to know that for someone to get tested, somebody has to pay for it. And here I am, after a KO loss, not even knowing what's next, just sitting around — and they come testing me.

"Of course it's possible ... but my imagination — my suspicious side — tells me: what if they wanted to get rid of me, like it was my fault? But it didn't work, because I'm a clean fighter. So after I got a negative result, a week later I received the release letter."

Gvozdyk confirmed that he also passed a drug test before the weigh-in.

His suspicions put to one side, Gvozdyk remains adamant that he was treated exactly to what he signed up for. But he is also acutely aware of his positioning in the sport as an aging former world champion, now with three losses on his ledger.

"I signed a contract, and they acted accordingly. I felt like an asset — but after the loss, I became a liability," he said.

Gvozdyk said he never met White — Zuffa Boxing's co-founder — in the flesh, but this lack of a personal touch hasn't dissuaded him of the opinion that Zuffa Boxing may be the perfect fit for the right fighter.

"Of course, it depends on the conditions. If numbers and everything looks right, I don't see why not," he said. "But I hope they don't go on to take over the sport. That won't be good for fighters. When fighters have fewer options, they will be forced to fight for less.

"At the moment their [Zuffa] title doesn't seem as prestigious as the others that we are used to. But give them some time. With big names like Shakur [Stevenson] signing, people will soon start recognizing its worth."

articles.title: DWCS 90 contract winner calls out King Green: 'I'd f*ck him up'
articles.summary: After scraping by for a contract win at DWCS 90, Adam Livingston had a bold callout for King Green, who he says "sucks."
articles.body:
LAS VEGAS – Adam Livingston is wasting no time gunning for established names at lightweight after his Dana White's Contender Series 90 contract win.

Livingsto (8-1 MMA, 0-0 UFC) barely escaped Tuesday's event with a UFC contract following a split decision win over Hunter Smith at Meta APEX. UFC CEO White seemed on the fence about giving him a contract, but ultimately rewarded him with one.

"I know I'm only 25, but I've been having this dream for a while," Livingston told MMA Junkie and other reporters post-fight at DWCS 90. "I'm very happy all my hard work paid off, especially against such a game opponent in Hunter Smith. I wish I could've finished him, but I had to play it smart. He has power in his hands so I played a smart fight. I still had some exciting moments in there. … I'm super happy I'm finally a UFC fighter. I've been wanting to say that for a f*cking long time."

With his place on the roster secure, Livingston isn't bringing a humble approach. He wants something big for his debut, and is calling for a spot on UFC's annual card at Madison Square Garden in New York, which this year is UFC 334 on Nov. 14, and he wants one of the most-tenured names at 155 pounds in King Green (36-17-1 MMA, 17-12-1 UFC), whom, despite a current four-fight winning streak, he doesn't think much of.

"I want to fight big names," Livingston said. "One person I really want to fight is Bobby Green. I think I'd f*ck him up. I think that'd be a great fight to put on at MSG down in New York. I want some big names and get back in there and fight. I'm only young for so long. I want to make some good money and put on awesome fights."

"That guy sucks, honestly. Before this fight I'm like, 'Hunter Smith is a tougher fight than Bobby Green.' He has his hands down and sh*t. I do that sometimes, but he's not a tall, lengthy guy like I am. I'd put his f*cking lights out. He's got to retire soon, so let's pass the torch to a young, hungry guy like me."
authors: Mike Bohn and Jeronimo Guerra, MMA Junkie

articles.title: Tyson Fury launches fresh swipe at Anthony Joshua as talks over fight continue
articles.summary: Tyson Fury says Anthony Joshua has been 'conning everybody for years' as he criticised his British rival yet again amid ongoing talks over a fight between the pair; Promoter Frank Warren said the ball is in Joshua's court, with the location of the fight remaining a defining talking point
articles.body:
Fury and Joshua had appeared closer than ever to agreeing a super-fight long-in-the-making, only for Saudi organisers Sela's wish to hold the event in the USA to emerge as a major stumbling block.

Joshua's side have maintained their desire for the fight to take place in the UK.

Fury took to Instagram once again on Wednesday to question the hold up.

"Joshua, where are you? Still no deal done. It's getting quite tiring," said Fury. "I've been down to fight in every location that's been mentioned - England, Ireland, Vegas, New York, back to England, back to Ireland, back to New York. I've said yep, yep, yep every single time with zero stipulations.

"The facts are that I feel like you're being a coward. I feel like you don't want the fight and you're just conning everybody. I feel like you've been doing that for years."

Joshua is coming off a second-round knockout victory over Kristian Prenga in July, during which he was notably floored twice in the first round.

Fury also last fought in July when he took on Mariusz Wach, with the 46-year-old retiring in the seventh round.

"You've had many opportunities to fight me, but deep down you've never really wanted it, so let's see if you're going to man out for a final time," Fury continued.

"We're both f***ing 37, 38 years old - let's f***ing fight. It's a boxing match and you've been banjoed before plenty of times.

"You've been knocked sparked out a few times. So what, what's the worst that can happen? I'm going to f***ing chin you, 100 per cent, but it's nothing that hasn't been done before!"

Promoter Frank Warren insisted Wednesday that the ball was "100 per cent" in Joshua's court.

"Tyson has signed up for the fight and agreed to the fight," said Warren. "He's all good to go, just waiting for AJ. I can't speak for him, because he's with Matchroom. He [Fury] has signed."

He did, meanwhile, admit he was uncertain as to the fight's location, with Fury having this week teased Madison Square Garden on social media.

"That I don't know," he continued. "That's going to be up to the people who are putting up the money and the promoters and the TV company putting up the money.

"Tyson just wants to get on. He said 'I don't care where I'll fight, whether it's Wembley, New York, Isle of Wight, Isle of Man - I'll fight him anywhere'. He doesn't care."

articles.title: Frank Warren responds to Chris Eubank Jr and Audley Harrison comments while backing Moses Itauma to come back stronger
articles.summary: Promoter Frank Warren says Moses Itauma proved he has heart and a great chin despite Saturday's stoppage defeat to Filip Hrgovic, downplaying criticism of the young heavyweight's preparations and backing him to go on and become world heavyweight champion.
articles.body:
The previously undefeated Itauma had seemingly been dominating the scorecards and on course to clinch the IBF belt at the age of just 21 at the weekend, only to drastically run out of steam as he was stopped in the ninth round by his Croatian counterpart.

It would prompt doubts over head coach Ben Davison from certain members of the boxing community, former Olympic champion Audley Harrison and Chris Eubank Jr among those questioning Itauma's tactics.

"I'm not commenting on any of that until I sit down with the team," Promoter Warren told Sky Sports. "They've got their opinions - they want to look at their own careers, we're worried about what Moses [Itauma] has done.

"Let's get it right you know, Audley Harrison, it just didn't happen for him. Chris Eubank is 36 years of age and he's never won a world title - in his last fight he was all over the place.

"They've got their opinions, they're entitled to them, but they all come out with their knives out afterwards but before the fight there wasn't anybody who tipped [Hrgovic] to win other things than his team."

Despite the outcome, Warren pointed to the fight as proof of both Itauma's heart and his chin after a battle of attrition against Hrgovic.

"As soon as that first bell went, he just put his foot on the throttle and put it into overdrive. That's how he fought and he didn't pace himself," Warren said.

"Obviously there's lessons to be learned and discussions to be had - lots of things to be sorted out. But he's 21 years of age and he was in with a good fighter, who only had one loss in his Olympic career.

"It is what it is and we can't change it, all we can do is learn from it. In my experience in the game, I know that there are a lot of things there we need to tweak and things that we need to do to put right.

"I genuinely believe he can go on to become a world champion and hold the title."

Warren maintained Itauma possesses the talent to come back stronger in his pursuit of a world title, referencing early defeats in the career of heavyweight great Wladimir Klitschko.

"The area is not to get him fit - just look at the pace of the fight and the amount of punches he's thrown, it's managing it and it's his fight management," Warren continued. "You haven't got to go full throttle every round and every punch you throw him, hasn't got to knock somebody over.

"If there's a wall and you've got a sledgehammer, you keep hitting it and hitting it. It doesn't always go and sometimes you've got to chip away at the foundations with a small hammer and it'll collapse.

"That's what he's got to learn and to use his talents and his skills - he will do that, I'm absolutely sure of it."

articles.title: Inside TNT's unlikely bet to 'revive boxing' for the U.S. masses, 1.6 million viewers later
articles.summary: TNT is the rare U.S. TV network these days willing to embrace boxing. After the first two events drew a combined 1.6 million viewers, top executives hope Fri...
articles.body:
TV executives do not exactly embrace boxing. They never have.

Boxing certainly does not elicit waves of warm hues with its politics, smattering of sanctioning bodies and reluctance of the best willing to fight the best. It is what has always bogged down the sport, relegating boxing to the farthest corners of the sporting universe, scrambling for audience scraps left by the NFL, NBA, MLB and the NHL.

Boxing once commanded a modicum of respect when it was televised with great success on Showtime and HBO. But once those cable giants decided to get out of the sport — HBO in 2018, and Showtime in 2023 — the sweet science became a TV orphan again. It was picked up sporadically by ESPN with its association with Top Rank, but otherwise had to find its niche with streaming providers DAZN, Prime Video and Paramount.

Now, hopefully, boxing may have found another TV home in TNT, after a deal was hammered out in April between DAZN and the Warner Brothers Discovery's TV network.

The partnership is contracted to run for a year, and it started out well, drawing 750,000 viewers, according to TNT, for its initial broadcast on July 4. That broadcast, of Abdullah Mason's defense of the WBO lightweight world championship against Albert Bell, peaked at 820,000 viewers between 11:45 p.m. and midnight ET.

The second show, on August 1, with William Zepeda winning the vacant WBC lightweight title over Lamont Roach Jr. and Raymond Muratalla retaining the IBF lightweight belt over Robson Conceicao, garnered a ratings high of 694,000 average viewers for the final two hours, peaking at 786,000 for the main event.

What may be even more promising looms this Friday, when TNT features stubby, 6-foot-2 Andy Ruiz and his everyman, fan-friendly style in a true David-vs.-Goliath brawl against towering 6-foot-7 Polish contender Damian Knyba at the Prudential Center in Newark, New Jersey.

Craig Barry, executive vice president and chief content officer for TNT Sports, was the prime factor in making the TNT deal with the DAZN. TNT now finds itself in rare company — the jutting oasis on the barren TV landscape that still televises boxing in the U.S..

But why boxing, when it seems every other network cannot run away fast enough from the sport?

"The truth of the matter is we have been looking for different opportunities to venture into contact sports, and we have always liked boxing, which stems way back to our [Warner Bros.] history with HBO boxing," Barry told Uncrowned. "We were looking at various opportunities and ones that existed. We came to the conclusion that boxing on cable at this current moment is nonexistent. You just couldn't get quality fights that were accessible for the boxing fan on what I would refer to as traditional cable.

"For us, that means streaming on [HBO] Max, and we have House of Highlights extending there. We felt if an opportunity presented itself, if we got some good fights, and we had the opportunity to build a franchise and a brand to revive boxing for the masses, we would be interested in doing that."

Barry felt if he could marry the fights with a studio show and a pre-fight programming package, it would create tentpole events, much like the way HBO did in the 1980s through the decades into the 2010s. His goal is to attract casual boxing fans. That means creating storylines and introducing fighters' backstories to a larger audience.

TNT has contracts with MLB and NHL, and has for decades produced the highly popular "Inside the NBA" studio show with Ernie Johnson, Charles Barkley, Shaquille O'Neal and Kenny Smith. Before and after NBA games, it was must-see TV for even casual NBA fans.

DAZN has international tentacles, but the other goal with this venture is to build a United States boxing brand. The sport could use it.

Boxing is still colossal internationally. The Filip Hrgovic vs. Moses Itauma IBF heavyweight title fight this past Saturday sold out the 20,000-seat O2 Arena in London, and captured national attention throughout England. If a fight of that magnitude took place in the U.S., it would be buried somewhere under the deluge of MLB scores, NFL training camp notes and any other morsel of sports news.

Getting fans familiarized with the fighters was part of the reason TNT built its boxing studio show, featuring host Adam Lefkoe, Hall of Famer Tim Bradley, future Hall of Famer Terence Crawford, and former world champion Shawn Porter. DAZN's ringside team of Todd Grisham, Sergio Mora and Chris Mannix handle the fight broadcasts.

"We don't rehearse anything," said Bradley, who used to work for ESPN and is the 2023 Boxing Writers Association of America Taub Award winner for excellence in boxing journalism. "I like the fact that there is structure, but there is no structure and I work best in that environment.

"It was a little different at ESPN. I loved ESPN, that was a well-oiled machine. But we would have meetings, and more meetings, and production meetings. We don't have that with TNT. They want us to be real and be ourselves. They want to make sure we do our homework, but the reaction is real and I'm a spontaneous person. Everything is real, not fabricated, and TNT wants us to be ourselves and flow — and I love that.

"I also like that TNT seems very committed to this," Bradley added. "No one would want to go into business with anyone for it to fail. We made big improvements from the first show to the second. Crawford and Shawn are very insightful. I come with experience, and Lefkoe is great at everything. Everyone is on the same page. Everyone wants boxing to succeed. Adam drives the ship. He is a great point guard. He doesn't care if he's the smartest guy in the room or not. What I like about Adam is he is very diverse, he can figure out anything."

Barry encourages the unapologetic studio approach. It's been a seamless transition between the DAZN's ringside squad and the studio commentary. Bradley is like the "Boxing Barkley," someone transparent and with no filter. Whatever is on his mind comes right out. There is also a chemistry — the quartet have text threads prior to the fights, sharing knowledge. It is a group that talks with its audience rather than at them.

The goal is to produce a quality product once a month. So far, TNT appears pleased.

"We are," Barry said. "I think the biggest surprise I have found is the buy-in from the boxing fans, the buy-in from our talent, the buy-in from the promotions. It feels everyone is on the same page to find success. Boxing fans are passionate. Our talent and the DAZN's talent get along very well. There is opportunity for friction [with egos], and we have not had any friction at all.

"We do our studio shows differently, leaning into that intersection between sport and culture. You see that on our hockey shows, and obviously on 'Inside the NBA.' The numbers we got for the first and second shows are respected numbers for any event, any MLB, NBA or NHL game. Standing something up from nothing is the hardest thing to do, right? We stood this thing up and people found boxing on TNT. Getting 750,000 on a cable network, that says you're building something. It says there is an opportunity there."

Ruiz vs. Knyba is a big deal — especially for TNT this Labor Day weekend. The network is hoping to exceed its benchmark 750,000 number, since Ruiz is a known former heavyweight world champion who comes with a layered backstory .

Ruiz, as a 25-to-1 underdog, shocked the world when he stopped the sculpted WBA/IBF/WBO heavyweight champion Anthony Joshua in the seventh round in June 2019. Ruiz has been his own worse enemy since then, jumping trainers, failing to train, almost eating his way out of boxing while enduring nagging injuries.

His world fell apart in the Joshua rematch, losing by unanimous decision in December 2019.

"Every fight changes a hero's journey," Lefkoe said. "It's a great storyline of Ruiz and Knyba. Knyba looks like he can be in 'The Odyssey' on that island with the huge humans. And you have this everyman, Ruiz, who is being promoted by Eddie Hearn, who produced the worst night of his life in the Joshua rematch. How much does Ruiz have left in the tank? It's going to be a learning lesson for all of us."

Terence Crawford has been a welcome addition to TNT's boxing coverage. (Bryan Bedder via Getty Images)
Former heavyweight champion Andy Ruiz Jr. headlines Friday's next TNT event. (Mark Robinson via Getty Images)

articles.title: Joshua vs Fury: Tyson Fury calls Anthony Joshua a 'coward' as wait continues
articles.summary: Tyson Fury says Anthony Joshua is a "coward" as the pair face a tense wait to see whether their long-awaited all-British heavyweight blockbuster can be agreed.
articles.body:
Tyson Fury has labelled Anthony Joshua a "coward" as the pair face a tense wait to see whether their long-awaited all-British heavyweight bout can be agreed.

The long-time rivals had been expected to finally settle their differences and face off in November, but the likelihood of that happening is diminishing as an agreement over the venue has yet to be reached.

Two-time unified world champion Joshua and his Matchroom promoter Eddie Hearn have signed a contract for the fight to take place in the United Kingdom, while the fight's organisers are understood to favour staging it in the United States.

Hearn has previously said the contracts would have to be renegotiated if the fight were to take place outside the United Kingdom.

On Wednesday, Fury, who defeated journeyman Mariusz Wach last month to keep the potential blockbuster clash with Joshua on track, said negotiations over the fight were becoming "quite tiring".

"I've been down to fight at every location that's been mentioned - England, Ireland, Vegas, New York, back to England, back to Ireland, back to New York," said the 38-year-old.

"Listen, I've said yep, yep, yep, yep, yep, every single time. Zero stipulations.

"The facts are I feel like you're being a coward. I feel like you don't want the fight and you're just conning everybody. I feel like you've been doing that for years.

"You've had many opportunities to fight me, but deep down you've never really wanted it, so let's see if you're going to man up for a final time."

In a separate post, Fury continued to taunt Joshua, 36, this time alongside former heavyweight champion Mike Tyson, telling his fellow Brit to "sign the contract, big boy" as he paid homage to Tyson's iconic line.

Queensbury's Frank Warren, who promotes Fury, told Sky Sports News his fighter was "100%" signed up for the fight.

"It is signed by Tyson," said Warren. "Tyson is signed up for the fight and agreed for the fight."

articles.title: Marlon Vera parts ways with long-time head coach Jason Parillo – ‘It was a hard decision’
articles.summary: “Chito” is changing things up. Former Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) Bantamweight title challenger Marlon Vera returns to action against rising contend...
articles.body:
Former Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) Bantamweight title challenger Marlon Vera returns to action against rising contender Charles Jourdain at UFC 331 later this month (Sat., Sept. 19, 2026) inside Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, California.

Vera is currently riding the first four-fight losing streak of his professional career, dropping consecutive decisions to Sean O'Malley , Deiveson Figueiredo , Aiemann Zahabi and, most recently, David Martinez .

"Chito" has not won a fight since Aug. 2023, when he defeated Pedro Munhoz via unanimous decision at UFC 292 .

Ahead of his pivotal UFC 331 return, Vera made the emotional decision to part ways with his longtime head coach, Jason Parillo .

"After the fight in Mexico, we went back to training, and I was trying to figure out what I needed — what wasn't allowing me to win these close decisions," Vera told Yahoo! Sports . "It was a hard decision because we didn't have a problem [with each other]. Nothing bad happened."

"I was asking myself what I could do moving forward to kill this bad streak and get back into the win column. I didn't want to let my career get to the very end and then question myself: 'What would have happened if I made a change?'"

There was no dramatic falling out between Vera and Parillo. Instead, "Chito" felt he owed it to himself to try something different before reaching the final stage of his career.

"Making changes is hard," Vera added. "You don't want to tell people you love or who have a big spot in your heart, 'Hey, I'm going to move forward for now and see what I can do.' It was a hard decision, but all I can do is try."

Vera began working with Parillo in 2018, and the respected striking coach helped guide him through the most successful period of his career. Their partnership included knockout victories over O'Malley, Frankie Edgar and Dominick Cruz ( watch highlights ), eventually culminating in Vera challenging O'Malley for the Bantamweight championship at UFC 299.

Unfortunately, the results have completely dried up since then.

While Vera remains one of the most durable fighters on the entire UFC roster — he has never been stopped in 36 professional appearances — his notoriously slow starts and inconsistent offensive output have repeatedly cost him on the judges' scorecards.

The 33-year-old is now training full-time alongside 21-year-old Bantamweight prospect Raul Rosas Jr. The team is using Vera's personal gym as its headquarters, while Rosas' father is overseeing the camp and organizing his training schedule.

Vera will attempt to prove the drastic change was worthwhile when he faces Jourdain, who has won three consecutive fights since dropping to Bantamweight.

So, while "Chito" has a new team and a fresh approach, UFC certainly didn't give him a soft landing.

With a fifth consecutive loss potentially putting his UFC future in jeopardy, Vera needs this one badly.

articles.title: The Katie Generation: Inside Ireland's boxing gyms, Katie Taylor's greatest legacy is everywhere
articles.summary: As one of boxing's all-time greats prepares to say farewell, a new generation of young women across Ireland and Northern Ireland are forging paths of their o...
articles.body:
When Katie Taylor leaves the ring on Saturday night , she will have a claim to being the greatest women's boxer in history.

GOAT debates in combat sports are often fruitless — beyond having to compare fighters from different weight classes, different levels of competition and different millennia, we're reliably confused by both recency bias and the glow of nostalgia. We find it hard to ignore charisma and correct for its absence. We're biased, hopelessly so, and there are far too many pitfalls on the landscape. So it is refreshing then, although incredibly rare, for a fighter in the debate to transcend the question altogether.

Maybe. Her staggering amateur career, culminating in Olympic gold in 2012, preceded a professional run that saw her become undisputed champion at two weight classes and dominate the lightweight division for years. She fought the best fighters of her generation, avenged her only loss, and of all her peers in the GOAT debate, she boasts the greatest singular win, defeating Amanda Serrano in an all-time classic firefight at Madison Square Garden in 2022. She went on to defeat Serrano twice more.

Others also have a claim. You might prefer earlier pioneers like Ann Wolfe or Laila Ali, or current multi-weight queen Claressa Shields. There are arguments for all.

Where there is no debate, however, is in the cultural impact Taylor has made on women's boxing, particularly in her home country of Ireland.

In this, she has no equal. Taylor entered the sport at a time when girls were barred from boxing — she would pretend to be a boy at local tournaments, tucking her hair into her headgear and fighting under the name "K. Taylor." Among all the accomplishments in her dazzling career, she takes the most pride in how far Irish boxing has come since then.

"Looking at the progress of women's boxing over the last 10 years, I think that is my greatest legacy," Taylor told Uncrowned's "The Ariel Helwani Show" earlier this week. "I just see every single boxing gym in the whole country here packed with female fighters, and I've even imagined in my mind's eye on Saturday night that many little girls will be there for the first time watching a boxing event. And maybe one of those little girls might fall in love with the sport and maybe they might surpass my achievements."

In the lead-up to Taylor's farewell, I traveled across Ireland and Northern Ireland to observe Katie's influence for myself — and as promised, I found gyms in every town filled with young women training alongside boys and men, chasing national titles, preparing for their first fights, or simply turning up each day because boxing runs deep through their family's history, as it does for many Irish families.

Some, barely 8 years old, wobbled around the gym in oversized headgear, still learning to keep their eyes open while throwing punches.

Others drifted effortlessly around the ring, snapping jabs back and forth, moving with all the ease and certainty of a teenage athlete coming into their own.

All of them were born after 2001, the year Taylor first stepped into the ring at the National Stadium in Dublin, for the first sanctioned women's boxing match in Ireland's history.

This Saturday, 25 years after that first fight, Taylor will enter the ring for the last time, just a few kilometers away at the iconic Croke Park in Dublin, leaving behind a vastly different landscape than the one she inherited.

Taylor famously battled for years to convince the International Olympic Committee that women's boxing was compelling enough to be included in the Olympics. On Saturday, 80,000 people will turn up to watch her fight in Dublin.

Among them are some of the young boxers photographed here. Keely Stevens from rural Charlestown was just 4 years old when Taylor won Olympic gold in 2012, and she has been grinding away on her own amateur journey ever since. Now 18, she'll be watching this Saturday with five national championships of her own under her belt.

Others are only beginning to discover what boxing might mean to them, having grown up in a world where Taylor was already fast becoming a national icon — and where the possibility of women in boxing could start to be taken for granted.

This is perhaps Taylor's greatest gift to the sport.

For years now, female inclusion in Irish boxing has not been a question, or a novelty, but rather a mark of pride for a people whose relationship with its fighters was already deep and storied.

Some gyms have even shifted their focus to primarily developing young women's fighters. St. Brigid's Boxing Club in Edenderry runs annual all-girls camps that attract hundreds of young boxers each year from more than 25 countries.

Here, and in clubs all across the island, the weight of Katie's presence is palpable.

Her face appears on walls and in old photo frames; her likeness sits alongside trophies and medals accumulated by the generations that have followed her.

As we take stock of Taylor's career in its final days, we'll be right to weigh her legacy in titles, Olympic medals, ticket sales. But its most powerful measure might be simpler.

Countless girls now stand in gyms who never had to question whether they belonged there.

From them will emerge the next Katie Taylor — and thousands of others will strive, in big ways and small, to find meaning in boxing.
